### pool diagnostics

```{r OLD}
############################################################
## HELPERS: Leave-One-Out (LOO) site-pool diagnostics
##
## Purpose
##   For each sample, compute incidence-based bookkeeping (a, b, c)
##   relative to the Leave-One-Out (LOO) site pool, then derive
##   diagnostic quantities that support the "distance-to-curve"
##   / "deviation-from-subset-expectation" workflow.
##
## Outputs (per-sample tibble)
##   - Sample, Site
##   - a, b, c                : Sørensen incidence components
##   - alpha                  : sample richness (a + b)
##   - gamma_loo              : LOO pool richness (a + c)
##   - f_loo                  : alpha / gamma_loo  (principled x-axis)
##   - overlap                : 1 - beta_sor(sample, LOO)  (observed y)
##   - y_exp                  : theoretical subset expectation = 2f/(1+f)
##   - delta                  : overlap - y_exp  (distance-to-curve)
##   - unique_frac            : b / alpha (fraction of sample unique vs LOO)
##   - b_count                : raw count of sample-unique taxa
##
## Notes
##   - All computations use incidence (presence/absence) data.
##   - Degenerate cases (empty LOO pool, empty sample) are handled and
##     returned as NA for the derived ratios to avoid division-by-zero.
##   - This function is intentionally explicit and easy to audit.
############################################################


# compute_loo_diagnostics -----------------------------------------------------
# comm_sampxtax : samples x taxa presence/absence matrix (rows = samples)
# sites          : character vector of site identifiers (length must equal nrow(comm))
# sample_names   : optional character vector of sample names (defaults to rownames(comm))
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per sample containing diagnostics described above.
############################################################
## HELPERS: Leave-One-Out (LOO) site-pool diagnostics
##
## Purpose
##   For each sample, compute incidence-based bookkeeping (a, b, c)
##   relative to the Leave-One-Out (LOO) site pool, then derive
##   diagnostic quantities that support the "distance-to-curve"
##   / "deviation-from-subset-expectation" workflow.
##
## Outputs (per-sample tibble)
##   - Sample, Site
##   - a, b, c                : Sørensen incidence components
##   - alpha                  : sample richness (a + b)
##   - gamma_loo              : LOO pool richness (a + c)
##   - f_loo                  : alpha / gamma_loo  (principled x-axis)
##   - overlap                : 1 - beta_sor(sample, LOO)  (observed y)
##   - y_exp                  : theoretical subset expectation = 2f/(1+f)
##   - delta                  : overlap - y_exp  (distance-to-curve)
##   - unique_frac            : b / alpha (fraction of sample unique vs LOO)
##   - b_count                : raw count of sample-unique taxa
##
## Notes
##   - All computations use incidence (presence/absence) data.
##   - Degenerate cases (empty LOO pool, empty sample) are handled and
##     returned as NA for the derived ratios to avoid division-by-zero.
##   - This function is intentionally explicit and easy to audit.
############################################################


# compute_loo_diagnostics -----------------------------------------------------
# comm_sampxtax : samples x taxa presence/absence matrix (rows = samples)
# sites          : character vector of site identifiers (length must equal nrow(comm))
# sample_names   : optional character vector of sample names (defaults to rownames(comm))
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per sample containing diagnostics described above.
compute_loo_diagnostics <- function(comm_sampxtax,
                                    sites,
                                    sample_names = rownames(comm_sampxtax)) {
  # Basic input checks --------------------------------------------------------
  # Ensure site labels match number of samples and that comm is a matrix/data.frame.
  stopifnot(length(sites) == nrow(comm_sampxtax))
  if (is.null(sample_names)) sample_names <- rownames(comm_sampxtax)
  stopifnot(length(sample_names) == nrow(comm_sampxtax))

  n <- nrow(comm_sampxtax)
  # Pre-allocate list for speed and safe binding later
  out <- vector("list", n)

  # Loop across samples: build LOO pool and compute a/b/c ----------------------
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    site_i <- sites[i]
    # indices of all samples in the same site
    idx_site <- which(sites == site_i)
    # indices of the LOO set (all other samples in site excluding focal)
    idx_loo  <- setdiff(idx_site, i)

    # If there are no other samples at the site (single-sample site),
    # return a row of NAs for the derived metrics (we cannot define a LOO pool).
    if (length(idx_loo) == 0) {
      out[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
        Sample = sample_names[i],
        Site = site_i,
        a = NA_integer_,    # shared presences (undefined)
        b = NA_integer_,    # sample-unique presences (undefined)
        c = NA_integer_,    # loo-unique presences (undefined)
        alpha = NA_integer_,
        gamma_loo = NA_integer_,
        f_loo = NA_real_,
        overlap = NA_real_,
        y_exp = NA_real_,
        delta = NA_real_,
        unique_frac = NA_real_,
        b_count = NA_integer_
      )
      next
    }

    # Convert sample and pool to integer 0/1 vectors (safe in case input is counts)
    samp_i  <- as.integer(comm_sampxtax[i, ] > 0)
    pool_loo <- as.integer(colSums(comm_sampxtax[idx_loo, , drop = FALSE]) > 0)

    # a, b, c incidence bookkeeping (Sørensen components) -----------------------
    # a = taxa present in both sample and loo-pool
    # b = taxa present in sample but absent from loo-pool (sample-unique)
    # c = taxa absent from sample but present in loo-pool (loo-unique)
    a <- sum(samp_i == 1 & pool_loo == 1)
    b <- sum(samp_i == 1 & pool_loo == 0)
    c <- sum(samp_i == 0 & pool_loo == 1)

    # Derived counts ----------------------------------------------------------
    alpha <- a + b               # sample richness
    gamma_loo <- a + c           # loo-pool richness

    # Principled x-axis: fraction relative to LOO pool -------------------------
    # If gamma_loo == 0 (no taxa observed in other samples), we cannot form f_loo
    if (gamma_loo == 0) {
      f_loo <- NA_real_
      y_exp <- NA_real_
    } else {
      f_loo <- alpha / gamma_loo
      # theoretical subset expectation for Sørensen overlap (no sample-unique taxa)
      # y_exp = 2f / (1 + f)  (derived from algebra when b = 0)
      y_exp <- 2 * f_loo / (1 + f_loo)
    }

    # Observed overlap (1 - Sørensen dissimilarity) ---------------------------
    # Sørensen (incidence) dissimilarity = (b + c) / (2a + b + c)
    # So 1 - beta_sor = 2a / (2a + b + c). If denominator is zero -> NA.
    denom <- (2 * a + b + c)
    overlap <- ifelse(denom == 0, NA_real_, 2 * a / denom)

    # Distance-to-curve: observed minus theoretical ---------------------------
    # delta > 0 : sample is more overlapped than expected (rare)
    # delta < 0 : sample falls below subset expectation -> indicates unique taxa / idiosyncrasy
    delta <- ifelse(is.na(overlap) | is.na(y_exp), NA_real_, overlap - y_exp)

    # Unique fraction within the sample (satellite load proxy)
    unique_frac <- ifelse(alpha == 0, NA_real_, b / alpha)

    # Pack row
    out[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      Sample = sample_names[i],
      Site = site_i,
      a = a,
      b = b,
      c = c,
      alpha = alpha,
      gamma_loo = gamma_loo,
      f_loo = f_loo,
      overlap = overlap,
      y_exp = y_exp,
      delta = delta,
      unique_frac = unique_frac,
      b_count = b
    )
  }

  # Bind and return a single tibble ------------------------------------------
  dplyr::bind_rows(out)
}


# compute_loo_from_physeq -----------------------------------------------------
# Convenience wrapper to run the diagnostics directly on a phyloseq-like object.
# ps       : phyloseq object (or similar) that works with your helper functions:
#            - phylo2vegan_sd(ps) -> sample_data as a data.frame with rownames = sample IDs
#            - get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps) -> samples x taxa PA matrix
# site_var : column name in sample_data that stores site identifiers
#
# Returns: diagnostic tibble from compute_loo_diagnostics()
compute_loo_from_physeq <- function(ps, site_var) {
  # Extract sample metadata (this follows the pattern used elsewhere in the pipeline)
  sd <- phylo2vegan_sd(ps) %>% dplyr::mutate(Sample = rownames(.))
  comm <- get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps)  # expected to be samples x taxa PA matrix
  # Defensive: ensure ordering matches (the lower-level function expects this)
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(sd), rownames(comm)))
  compute_loo_diagnostics(comm, sites = sd[[site_var]], sample_names = sd$Sample)
}


# summarize_states ------------------------------------------------------------
# Summarize diagnostic metrics at the state level for reporting / tables.
# diag_df    : data.frame/tibble returned by compute_loo_diagnostics()
# state_col  : name of the column to group by (default "Site" / "State")
# delta_eps  : threshold for "meaningful" negative deviation (default 0.05)
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per state and summary statistics useful for text.
summarize_loo_states <- function(diag_df, state_col = "Site", delta_eps = 0.05) {
  # Group by state_col and compute interpretable summaries
  diag_df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!rlang::sym(state_col)) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      # sample count with valid delta (useful to filter tiny states)
      n = sum(!is.na(delta)),

      # central tendency of deviation from the theoretical curve
      median_delta = median(delta, na.rm = TRUE),

      # mean negative deviation: average amount samples fall below the theoretical curve
      # pmin(delta, 0) ensures positive deviations do not inflate this metric.
      mean_neg_delta = mean(pmin(delta, 0), na.rm = TRUE),

      # fraction of samples falling more than `delta_eps` below the theoretical curve.
      # This is an intuitive frequency metric (e.g., "20% of samples fall >5% below expectation")
      frac_below_eps = mean(delta < -delta_eps, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median proportion of sample taxa that are unique relative to LOO pool
      median_unique_frac = median(unique_frac, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median LOO-fraction (alpha / gamma_loo) - gives a sense of sampling depth
      median_f_loo = median(f_loo, na.rm = TRUE),

      # association between unique_frac and delta (Spearman rank correlation).
      # Only compute when there are enough samples to give a stable estimate (>= 5 valid pairs).
      spearman_rho_unique_delta = ifelse(
        sum(!is.na(unique_frac) & !is.na(delta)) >= 5,
        cor(unique_frac, delta, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
        NA_real_
      ),

      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    # Make the grouping column have a standard name "State" for downstream code.
    dplyr::rename(State = !!rlang::sym(state_col))
}


############################################################
## EXAMPLE USAGE (copy-paste into your script)
##
## # Per-kingdom diagnostics
## diag_fun <- compute_loo_from_physeq(ps_fungi_std, site_var = "Site")
## diag_bac <- compute_loo_from_physeq(ps_bac_std,  site_var = "Site")
##
## # State-level summaries (for Results table / short reporting)
## state_summ_fun <- summarize_loo_states(diag_fun, state_col = "Site", delta_eps = 0.05)
## state_summ_bac <- summarize_loo_states(diag_bac,  state_col = "Site", delta_eps = 0.05)
##
## # Quick checks / diagnostics:
## #  - How many samples had degenerate LOO pools?
## sum(is.na(diag_fun$f_loo))
## #  - Distribution of delta:
## hist(diag_fun$delta, breaks = 50)
## #  - Delta vs unique fraction (pooled)
## ggplot(diag_fun, aes(x = unique_frac, y = delta)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
##   geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE)
##
## # Suggested final figure (per-state, per-kingdom):
## #  - x: f_loo (alpha / gamma_loo)
## #  - y: overlap
## #  - points: samples
## #  - lines: theoretical curve (y_exp), empirical state slope, dashed 1:1 for reference
## #  - annotation: mean_neg_delta & median_unique_frac in top-right of each facet
############################################################


############################################################
## IMPLEMENTATION NOTES / COMMENTARY (for manuscript & reproducibility)
##
## 1) Why f_loo vs alpha/gamma_site:
##    - f_loo = alpha / gamma_loo is the principled x-axis for the subset curve.
##      gamma_site includes focal-sample taxa and thus inflates the denominator
##      in ways that break the exact algebraic expectation. If you must keep
##      alpha/gamma_site for consistency with earlier figures, compute f_loo
##      in parallel and present the theoretical curve relative to f_loo (or
##      include both axes in supplementary materials).
##
## 2) Interpretation of delta:
##    - delta = overlap - y_exp. Negative values indicate sample-unique taxa
##      or compositional mismatch beyond simple subsampling. Use mean_neg_delta
##      and frac_below_eps as compact summaries.
##
## 3) Handling degenerate cases:
##    - Sites with a single sample produce NA diagnostics. Report how many
##      such sites exist and consider excluding them from state-level summaries.
##
## 4) Sensitivity checks:
##    - Try alternative thresholds for frac_below_eps (0.05, 0.1).
##    - Check whether removing very-low-richness samples changes state summaries.
##
## 5) Linking to core/satellite bookkeeping:
##    - The `b` and `b_count` fields are directly useful for your core/satellite
##      analyses. Compare `b_count` and `unique_frac` to the per-sample number
##      of taxa classified as "satellite" by your prevalence threshold. A tight
##      positive relationship supports the satellite-driven interpretation.
############################################################


# compute_loo_from_physeq -----------------------------------------------------
# Convenience wrapper to run the diagnostics directly on a phyloseq-like object.
# ps       : phyloseq object (or similar) that works with your helper functions:
#            - phylo2vegan_sd(ps) -> sample_data as a data.frame with rownames = sample IDs
#            - get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps) -> samples x taxa PA matrix
# site_var : column name in sample_data that stores site identifiers
#
# Returns: diagnostic tibble from compute_loo_diagnostics()
compute_loo_from_physeq <- function(ps, site_var) {
  # Extract sample metadata (this follows the pattern used elsewhere in the pipeline)
  sd <- phylo2vegan_sd(ps) %>% dplyr::mutate(Sample = rownames(.))
  comm <- get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps)  # expected to be samples x taxa PA matrix
  # Defensive: ensure ordering matches (the lower-level function expects this)
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(sd), rownames(comm)))
  compute_loo_diagnostics(comm, sites = sd[[site_var]], sample_names = sd$Sample)
}


# summarize_loo_states ------------------------------------------------------------
# Summarize diagnostic metrics at the state level for reporting / tables.
# diag_df    : data.frame/tibble returned by compute_loo_diagnostics()
# state_col  : name of the column to group by (default "Site" / "State")
# delta_eps  : threshold for "meaningful" negative deviation (default 0.05)
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per state and summary statistics useful for text.
summarize_loo_states <- function(diag_df, state_col = "Site", delta_eps = 0.05) {
  # Group by state_col and compute interpretable summaries
  diag_df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!rlang::sym(state_col)) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      # sample count with valid delta (useful to filter tiny states)
      n = sum(!is.na(delta)),

      # central tendency of deviation from the theoretical curve
      median_delta = median(delta, na.rm = TRUE),

      # mean negative deviation: average amount samples fall below the theoretical curve
      # pmin(delta, 0) ensures positive deviations do not inflate this metric.
      mean_neg_delta = mean(pmin(delta, 0), na.rm = TRUE),

      # fraction of samples falling more than `delta_eps` below the theoretical curve.
      # This is an intuitive frequency metric (e.g., "20% of samples fall >5% below expectation")
      frac_below_eps = mean(delta < -delta_eps, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median proportion of sample taxa that are unique relative to LOO pool
      median_unique_frac = median(unique_frac, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median LOO-fraction (alpha / gamma_loo) - gives a sense of sampling depth
      median_f_loo = median(f_loo, na.rm = TRUE),

      # association between unique_frac and delta (Spearman rank correlation).
      # Only compute when there are enough samples to give a stable estimate (>= 5 valid pairs).
      spearman_rho_unique_delta = ifelse(
        sum(!is.na(unique_frac) & !is.na(delta)) >= 5,
        cor(unique_frac, delta, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
        NA_real_
      ),

      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    # Make the grouping column have a standard name "State" for downstream code.
    dplyr::rename(State = !!rlang::sym(state_col))
}
```

```{r}
############################################################
## HELPERS: Leave-One-Out (LOO) site-pool diagnostics
##
## Purpose
##   For each sample, compute incidence-based bookkeeping (a, b, c)
##   relative to the Leave-One-Out (LOO) site pool, then derive
##   diagnostic quantities that support the "distance-to-curve"
##   / "deviation-from-subset-expectation" workflow.
##
## Outputs (per-sample tibble)
##   - Sample, Site
##   - a, b, c                : Sørensen incidence components
##   - alpha                  : sample richness (a + b)
##   - gamma_loo              : LOO pool richness (a + c)
##   - f_loo                  : alpha / gamma_loo  (principled x-axis)
##   - overlap                : 1 - beta_sor(sample, LOO)  (observed y)
##   - y_exp                  : theoretical subset expectation = 2f/(1+f)
##   - delta                  : overlap - y_exp  (distance-to-curve)
##   - unique_frac            : b / alpha (fraction of sample unique vs LOO)
##   - b_count                : raw count of sample-unique taxa
##
## Notes
##   - All computations use incidence (presence/absence) data.
##   - Degenerate cases (empty LOO pool, empty sample) are handled and
##     returned as NA for the derived ratios to avoid division-by-zero.
##   - This function is intentionally explicit and easy to audit.
############################################################


# compute_loo_diagnostics -----------------------------------------------------
# comm_sampxtax : samples x taxa presence/absence matrix (rows = samples)
# sites          : character vector of site identifiers (length must equal nrow(comm))
# sample_names   : optional character vector of sample names (defaults to rownames(comm))
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per sample containing diagnostics described above.
compute_loo_diagnostics <- function(comm_sampxtax,
                                    sites,
                                    sample_names = rownames(comm_sampxtax)) {
  # Basic input checks --------------------------------------------------------
  # Ensure site labels match number of samples and that comm is a matrix/data.frame.
  stopifnot(length(sites) == nrow(comm_sampxtax))
  if (is.null(sample_names)) sample_names <- rownames(comm_sampxtax)
  stopifnot(length(sample_names) == nrow(comm_sampxtax))

  n <- nrow(comm_sampxtax)
  # Pre-allocate list for speed and safe binding later
  out <- vector("list", n)

  # Loop across samples: build LOO pool and compute a/b/c ----------------------
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    site_i <- sites[i]
    # indices of all samples in the same site
    idx_site <- which(sites == site_i)
    # indices of the LOO set (all other samples in site excluding focal)
    idx_loo  <- setdiff(idx_site, i)

    # If there are no other samples at the site (single-sample site),
    # return a row of NAs for the derived metrics (we cannot define a LOO pool).
    if (length(idx_loo) == 0) {
      out[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
        Sample = sample_names[i],
        Site = site_i,
        a = NA_integer_,    # shared presences (undefined)
        b = NA_integer_,    # sample-unique presences (undefined)
        c = NA_integer_,    # loo-unique presences (undefined)
        alpha = NA_integer_,
        gamma_loo = NA_integer_,
        f_loo = NA_real_,
        overlap = NA_real_,
        y_exp = NA_real_,
        delta = NA_real_,
        unique_frac = NA_real_,
        b_count = NA_integer_
      )
      next
    }

    # Convert sample and pool to integer 0/1 vectors (safe in case input is counts)
    samp_i  <- as.integer(comm_sampxtax[i, ] > 0)
    pool_loo <- as.integer(colSums(comm_sampxtax[idx_loo, , drop = FALSE]) > 0)

    # a, b, c incidence bookkeeping (Sørensen components) -----------------------
    # a = taxa present in both sample and loo-pool
    # b = taxa present in sample but absent from loo-pool (sample-unique)
    # c = taxa absent from sample but present in loo-pool (loo-unique)
    a <- sum(samp_i == 1 & pool_loo == 1)
    b <- sum(samp_i == 1 & pool_loo == 0)
    c <- sum(samp_i == 0 & pool_loo == 1)

    # Derived counts ----------------------------------------------------------
    alpha <- a + b               # sample richness
    gamma_loo <- a + c           # loo-pool richness

    # Principled x-axis: fraction relative to LOO pool -------------------------
    # If gamma_loo == 0 (no taxa observed in other samples), we cannot form f_loo
    if (gamma_loo == 0) {
      f_loo <- NA_real_
      y_exp <- NA_real_
    } else {
      f_loo <- alpha / gamma_loo
      # theoretical subset expectation for Sørensen overlap (no sample-unique taxa)
      # y_exp = 2f / (1 + f)  (derived from algebra when b = 0)
      y_exp <- 2 * f_loo / (1 + f_loo)
    }

    # Observed overlap (1 - Sørensen dissimilarity) ---------------------------
    # Sørensen (incidence) dissimilarity = (b + c) / (2a + b + c)
    # So 1 - beta_sor = 2a / (2a + b + c). If denominator is zero -> NA.
    denom <- (2 * a + b + c)
    overlap <- ifelse(denom == 0, NA_real_, 2 * a / denom)

    # Distance-to-curve: observed minus theoretical ---------------------------
    # delta > 0 : sample is more overlapped than expected (rare)
    # delta < 0 : sample falls below subset expectation -> indicates unique taxa / idiosyncrasy
    delta <- ifelse(is.na(overlap) | is.na(y_exp), NA_real_, overlap - y_exp)

    # Unique fraction within the sample (satellite load proxy)
    unique_frac <- ifelse(alpha == 0, NA_real_, b / alpha)

    # Pack row
    out[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      Sample = sample_names[i],
      Site = site_i,
      a = a,
      b = b,
      c = c,
      alpha = alpha,
      gamma_loo = gamma_loo,
      f_loo = f_loo,
      overlap = overlap,
      y_exp = y_exp,
      delta = delta,
      unique_frac = unique_frac,
      b_count = b
    )
  }

  # Bind and return a single tibble ------------------------------------------
  dplyr::bind_rows(out)
}


# compute_loo_from_physeq -----------------------------------------------------
# Convenience wrapper to run the diagnostics directly on a phyloseq-like object.
# ps       : phyloseq object (or similar) that works with your helper functions:
#            - phylo2vegan_sd(ps) -> sample_data as a data.frame with rownames = sample IDs
#            - get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps) -> samples x taxa PA matrix
# site_var : column name in sample_data that stores site identifiers
#
# Returns: diagnostic tibble from compute_loo_diagnostics()
compute_loo_from_physeq <- function(ps, site_var) {
  # Extract sample metadata (this follows the pattern used elsewhere in the pipeline)
  sd <- phylo2vegan_sd(ps) %>% dplyr::mutate(Sample = rownames(.))
  comm <- get_comm_pa_sampxtax(ps)  # expected to be samples x taxa PA matrix
  # Defensive: ensure ordering matches (the lower-level function expects this)
  stopifnot(identical(rownames(sd), rownames(comm)))
  compute_loo_diagnostics(comm, sites = sd[[site_var]], sample_names = sd$Sample)
}


# summarize_loo_states ------------------------------------------------------------
# Summarize diagnostic metrics at the state level for reporting / tables.
# diag_df    : data.frame/tibble returned by compute_loo_diagnostics()
# state_col  : name of the column to group by (default "Site" / "State")
# delta_eps  : threshold for "meaningful" negative deviation (default 0.05)
#
# Returns: tibble with one row per state and summary statistics useful for text.
summarize_loo_states <- function(diag_df, state_col = "Site", delta_eps = 0.05) {
  # Group by state_col and compute interpretable summaries
  diag_df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(!!rlang::sym(state_col)) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      # sample count with valid delta (useful to filter tiny states)
      n = sum(!is.na(delta)),

      # central tendency of deviation from the theoretical curve
      median_delta = median(delta, na.rm = TRUE),

      # mean negative deviation: average amount samples fall below the theoretical curve
      # pmin(delta, 0) ensures positive deviations do not inflate this metric.
      mean_neg_delta = mean(pmin(delta, 0), na.rm = TRUE),

      # fraction of samples falling more than `delta_eps` below the theoretical curve.
      # This is an intuitive frequency metric (e.g., "20% of samples fall >5% below expectation")
      frac_below_eps = mean(delta < -delta_eps, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median proportion of sample taxa that are unique relative to LOO pool
      median_unique_frac = median(unique_frac, na.rm = TRUE),

      # median LOO-fraction (alpha / gamma_loo) - gives a sense of sampling depth
      median_f_loo = median(f_loo, na.rm = TRUE),

      # association between unique_frac and delta (Spearman rank correlation).
      # Only compute when there are enough samples to give a stable estimate (>= 5 valid pairs).
      spearman_rho_unique_delta = ifelse(
        sum(!is.na(unique_frac) & !is.na(delta)) >= 5,
        cor(unique_frac, delta, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"),
        NA_real_
      ),

      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    # Make the grouping column have a standard name "State" for downstream code.
    dplyr::rename(State = !!rlang::sym(state_col))
}
```

## α–β coupling: Differentiation within states is not reducible to richness gradients

Table: per-state slopes/correlations for:

β_sor vs \|Δα_total\|

β_sim vs \|Δα_total\|

and same for \|Δα_core\|, \|Δα_sat\|

Figure: a summary (e.g., slope or R² heatmap; or forest-style dot plot)

Optional SI: α-preserving null summaries (if you run the null)

Below is a compilation layer that assumes you store a coupling object as attr(out, "alpha_beta_coupling") and that it contains a tidy summary_tbl (if it doesn’t yet, this code will just return NULL and you’ll see the “not coded yet” note).

```{r}
# ============================================================
# α–β coupling extraction and compilation
# ============================================================

tidy_one_coupling <- function(cpl, state_id) {
  # cpl is attr(out, "alpha_beta_coupling")
  if (is.null(cpl)) return(NULL)

  # Expect cpl$models is a named list like:
  # "sor_full__d_alpha_total", "sim_full__d_alpha_sat", etc.
  mods <- cpl$models
  if (is.null(mods) || length(mods) == 0) return(NULL)

  out <- purrr::imap_dfr(mods, function(fit, nm) {
    if (is.null(fit)) return(NULL)

    # parse names like: "<beta>__<alpha>"
    parts <- strsplit(nm, "__", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    if (length(parts) != 2) {
      beta_nm <- nm
      alpha_nm <- NA_character_
    } else {
      beta_nm <- parts[1]
      alpha_nm <- parts[2]
    }

    sm <- summary(fit)
    coefs <- coef(sm)
    # d_alpha is predictor; assume it is the 2nd row
    slope <- NA_real_
    pval  <- NA_real_
    if (nrow(coefs) >= 2) {
      slope <- coefs[2, "Estimate"]
      pval  <- coefs[2, "Pr(>|t|)"]
    }

    tibble::tibble(
      State = state_id,
      beta_metric = beta_nm,
      alpha_contrast = alpha_nm,
      slope = slope,
      p_value = pval,
      r2 = sm$r.squared,
      n_pairs = stats::df.residual(fit) + 2
    )
  })

  out
}

compile_alpha_beta_coupling <- function(state_tbl) {
  # state_tbl: tibble of per-state summary rows (bind_rows outputs)
  # Each row has attrs; we need the original row objects (list-column) OR rerun list
  # Preferred: pass a named list of per-state outputs instead (fungal_state_list).
  stop("Use compile_alpha_beta_coupling_from_list() with a state list.")
}

compile_alpha_beta_coupling_from_list <- function(state_list) {
  # state_list is a named list: names are State IDs; values are out rows with attrs
  purrr::imap_dfr(state_list, function(one_state_out, st) {
    cpl <- attr(one_state_out, "alpha_beta_coupling")
    tidy_one_coupling(cpl, st)
  })
}


alpha_beta_tbl <- compile_alpha_beta_coupling_from_list(fungal_state_list)

# quick sort: strongest coupling between βsor and |Δα_sat|
alpha_beta_tbl %>%
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^sor_", beta_metric)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(p_value)
```

```{r}
############################################################
## PART 2.5: compile α–β coupling summaries across states
##
## Requirement
##   Each state row must have attribute "alpha_beta_coupling"
##   with a component "summary_tbl" (tidy) containing at least:
##     - delta_component: alpha_total / alpha_core / alpha_sat
##     - beta_metric: sor_full / sim_full / sne_full (or similar)
##     - slope, r2, p (names are up to you)
##
## If current coupling object doesn't have summary_tbl yet:
##   -> NOT CODED YET: add it to pairwise_alpha_beta_coupling()
############################################################

compile_alpha_beta_coupling_tbl <- function(state_tbl) {
  if (is.null(state_tbl) || !is.data.frame(state_tbl) || !"State" %in% names(state_tbl)) return(NULL)

  bind_rows(lapply(state_tbl$State, function(st) {
    row <- get_state_row(state_tbl, st)
    cpl <- get_attr(row, "alpha_beta_coupling", default = NULL)

    if (is.null(cpl) || is.null(cpl$summary_tbl)) return(NULL)

    cpl$summary_tbl %>%
      mutate(State = st)
  }))
}
```

#### coupling summary now (if not in summary_tbl)

minimal summary_tbl builder that to add inside your pairwise_alpha_beta_coupling() (or wrap around its output). This summarizes per-state slope + R² for each pairing.

```{r}
############################################################
## NOT-CODED-YET BRIDGE: minimal coupling summary_tbl builder
## If pairwise_alpha_beta_coupling() currently returns only a pairwise table,
## use this helper to summarize it.
############################################################

summarize_coupling_pairwise <- function(pair_df,
                                       beta_cols = c("sor_full","sim_full","sne_full"),
                                       delta_cols = c("abs_dalpha_total","abs_dalpha_core","abs_dalpha_sat")) {
  if (is.null(pair_df) || !is.data.frame(pair_df)) return(NULL)

  out <- list()
  k <- 1
  for (b in beta_cols) {
    for (d in delta_cols) {
      if (!all(c(b, d) %in% names(pair_df))) next
      df <- pairwise_tbl %>% filter(is.finite(.data[[b]]), is.finite(.data[[d]]))
      if (nrow(df) < 20) next

      m <- lm(df[[b]] ~ df[[d]])
      sm <- summary(m)

      out[[k]] <- tibble(
        beta_metric = b,
        delta_component = d,
        slope = unname(coef(m)[2]),
        r2 = sm$r.squared,
        p = sm$coefficients[2,4],
        n_pairs = nrow(df)
      )
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  bind_rows(out)
}

summarize_coupling_pairwise(pair_df,
                                       beta_cols = c("sor_full","sim_full","sne_full"),
                                       delta_cols = c("abs_dalpha_total","abs_dalpha_core","abs_dalpha_sat"))
```

```{r}
plot_coupling_slopes <- function(coupling_tbl) {
  if (is.null(coupling_tbl) || nrow(coupling_tbl) == 0) return(NULL)

  ggplot(coupling_tbl, aes(x = delta_component, y = slope)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +

    theme_bw() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(x = "|Δα| component", y = "Slope of β ~ |Δα|")
}
```

## Host effects

```{r}
# ============================================================
# Full “battery” to test host-structure (means, variance, tails,
# distributions, conditional subsets) for BOTH satellites + core
# across ALL states in fungal_state_list
# ============================================================

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)

# ----------------------------
# Helpers
# ----------------------------

# Extract per-state pairwise df safely
get_pair_df <- function(x) {
  attr(x, "pairwise_df")
}

# Generic host-effect summary for a given beta column (e.g., "sor_sat", "sor_core")
host_effect_summary <- function(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = TRUE) {
  if (is.null(pair_df)) return(NULL)
  need <- c("same_site", "same_host", beta_col)
  if (!all(need %in% names(pair_df))) return(NULL)

  df <- pair_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[beta_col]]), !is.na(same_host))

  if (within_site) df <- df %>% filter(same_site)

  if (nrow(df) == 0 || dplyr::n_distinct(df$same_host) < 2) {
    return(tibble(
      n_pairs = nrow(df),
      mean_same = NA_real_, mean_diff = NA_real_,
      delta_diff_minus_same = NA_real_,
      sd_same = NA_real_, sd_diff = NA_real_,
      iqr_same = NA_real_, iqr_diff = NA_real_
    ))
  }

  summ <- df %>%
    group_by(same_host) %>%
    summarise(
      n_pairs = n(),
      mean_beta = mean(.data[[beta_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      sd_beta   = sd(.data[[beta_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      iqr_beta  = IQR(.data[[beta_col]], na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )

  mean_same <- summ %>% filter(same_host) %>% pull(mean_beta)
  mean_diff <- summ %>% filter(!same_host) %>% pull(mean_beta)

  sd_same <- summ %>% filter(same_host) %>% pull(sd_beta)
  sd_diff <- summ %>% filter(!same_host) %>% pull(sd_beta)

  iqr_same <- summ %>% filter(same_host) %>% pull(iqr_beta)
  iqr_diff <- summ %>% filter(!same_host) %>% pull(iqr_beta)

  tibble(
    n_pairs = sum(summ$n_pairs),
    mean_same = mean_same,
    mean_diff = mean_diff,
    delta_diff_minus_same = mean_diff - mean_same,
    sd_same = sd_same,
    sd_diff = sd_diff,
    iqr_same = iqr_same,
    iqr_diff = iqr_diff
  )
}

# Permutation test on mean difference (diff-host minus same-host)
perm_test_host_effect <- function(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = TRUE, nperm = 999) {
  if (is.null(pair_df)) return(NA_real_)
  need <- c("same_site", "same_host", beta_col)
  if (!all(need %in% names(pair_df))) return(NA_real_)

  df <- pair_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[beta_col]]), !is.na(same_host))

  if (within_site) df <- df %>% filter(same_site)

  if (nrow(df) == 0 || dplyr::n_distinct(df$same_host) < 2) return(NA_real_)

  y <- df[[beta_col]]
  g <- df$same_host

  obs <- mean(y[!g]) - mean(y[g])

  perm <- replicate(nperm, {
    gp <- sample(g)
    mean(y[!gp]) - mean(y[gp])
  })

  mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))
}

# Tail enrichment: is same-host enriched among lowest-q quantile of beta?
tail_enrichment <- function(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = TRUE, q = 0.10) {
  if (is.null(pair_df)) return(NULL)
  need <- c("same_site", "same_host", beta_col)
  if (!all(need %in% names(pair_df))) return(NULL)

  df <- pair_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[beta_col]]), !is.na(same_host))

  if (within_site) df <- df %>% filter(same_site)

  if (nrow(df) == 0 || dplyr::n_distinct(df$same_host) < 2) {
    return(tibble(
      q = q,
      prop_low_same = NA_real_,
      prop_low_diff = NA_real_,
      enrich_ratio_same_over_diff = NA_real_
    ))
  }

  thr <- quantile(df[[beta_col]], q, na.rm = TRUE)
  df <- df %>% mutate(low_beta = .data[[beta_col]] < thr)

  prop_low_same <- df %>% filter(same_host) %>% summarise(p = mean(low_beta)) %>% pull(p)
  prop_low_diff <- df %>% filter(!same_host) %>% summarise(p = mean(low_beta)) %>% pull(p)

  tibble(
    q = q,
    prop_low_same = prop_low_same,
    prop_low_diff = prop_low_diff,
    enrich_ratio_same_over_diff = ifelse(is.finite(prop_low_diff) && prop_low_diff > 0,
                                         prop_low_same / prop_low_diff, NA_real_)
  )
}

# Distribution comparison: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (same vs diff host)
# This tests "different distributions", not means.
ks_test_host <- function(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = TRUE) {
  if (is.null(pair_df)) return(NULL)
  need <- c("same_site", "same_host", beta_col)
  if (!all(need %in% names(pair_df))) return(NULL)

  df <- pair_df %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[beta_col]]), !is.na(same_host))

  if (within_site) df <- df %>% filter(same_site)

  y_same <- df %>% filter(same_host) %>% pull(.data[[beta_col]])
  y_diff <- df %>% filter(!same_host) %>% pull(.data[[beta_col]])

  if (length(y_same) < 10 || length(y_diff) < 10) {
    return(tibble(ks_D = NA_real_, ks_p = NA_real_, note = "too few pairs for KS"))
  }

  ks <- suppressWarnings(stats::ks.test(y_same, y_diff))
  tibble(ks_D = as.numeric(ks$statistic), ks_p = ks$p.value, note = NA_character_)
}

# Conditional subsets: run the same battery on a subset of pairs
# subset_expr should be something like quote(pair_type == "same_site_diff_host") etc.
run_battery_one <- function(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = TRUE, nperm = 999, q = 0.10) {
  out1 <- host_effect_summary(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = within_site)
  out2 <- tibble(p_perm = perm_test_host_effect(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = within_site, nperm = nperm))
  out3 <- tail_enrichment(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = within_site, q = q)
  out4 <- ks_test_host(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = within_site)
  bind_cols(out1, out2, out3, out4)
}

# ----------------------------
# Run across ALL states for BOTH components (sat + core)
# ----------------------------

run_host_battery_all_states <- function(fungal_state_list,
                                       beta_cols = c(sat = "sor_sat", core = "sor_core"),
                                       within_site = TRUE,
                                       nperm = 999,
                                       q = 0.10) {

  map_dfr(fungal_state_list, function(x) {

    State <- as.character(x$State[[1]])
    pair_df <- get_pair_df(x)

    # Optional: attach pair_type if present in your pair_df (it usually is)
    # If not present, you can build it from same_site/same_host flags.
    if (!is.null(pair_df) && !("pair_type" %in% names(pair_df)) &&
        all(c("same_site", "same_host") %in% names(pair_df))) {

      pair_df <- pair_df %>%
        mutate(pair_type = dplyr::case_when(
          same_site & same_host ~ "same_site_same_host",
          same_site & !same_host ~ "same_site_diff_host",
          !same_site & same_host ~ "diff_site_same_host",
          TRUE ~ "diff_site_diff_host"
        ))
    }

    # Run for each requested beta column (sat/core)
    res <- imap_dfr(beta_cols, function(beta_col, label) {
      if (is.null(pair_df) || !(beta_col %in% names(pair_df))) {
        return(tibble(
          State = State, component = label, beta_col = beta_col,
          n_pairs = NA_integer_,
          mean_same = NA_real_, mean_diff = NA_real_, delta_diff_minus_same = NA_real_,
          sd_same = NA_real_, sd_diff = NA_real_, iqr_same = NA_real_, iqr_diff = NA_real_,
          p_perm = NA_real_,
          q = q, prop_low_same = NA_real_, prop_low_diff = NA_real_, enrich_ratio_same_over_diff = NA_real_,
          ks_D = NA_real_, ks_p = NA_real_, note = "missing pair_df or beta column"
        ))
      }

      b <- run_battery_one(pair_df, beta_col, within_site = within_site, nperm = nperm, q = q)

      tibble(
        State = State,
        component = label,
        beta_col = beta_col
      ) %>%
        bind_cols(b)
    })

    res
  })
}

battery_tbl <- run_host_battery_all_states(
  fungal_state_list = fungal_state_list,
  beta_cols = c(sat = "sor_sat", core = "sor_core"),
  within_site = TRUE,
  nperm = 999,
  q = 0.10
)

core_host_effect_by_site <- map_dfr(fungal_state_list, function(x) {

  State <- as.character(x$State[[1]])
  df <- attr(x, "pairwise_df")
  if (is.null(df)) return(NULL)

  df %>%
    filter(same_site, !is.na(sor_core)) %>%
    mutate(site = site_i) %>%         # since same_site, site_i == site_j
    group_by(site) %>%
    summarise(
      n_pairs = n(),
      n_same = sum(same_host),
      n_diff = sum(!same_host),
      mean_same = mean(sor_core[same_host], na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_diff = mean(sor_core[!same_host], na.rm = TRUE),
      delta = mean_diff - mean_same,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    filter(n_same > 0, n_diff > 0) %>%
    mutate(State = State)
})

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

core_host_specific_contrasts <- map_dfr(fungal_state_list, function(x) {

  State <- as.character(x$State[[1]])
  df <- attr(x, "pairwise_df")
  if (is.null(df)) return(NULL)

  # need these
  need <- c("same_site", "host_i", "host_j", "sor_core")
  if (!all(need %in% names(df))) return(NULL)

  dfw <- df %>%
    filter(same_site, !is.na(sor_core)) %>%
    mutate(
      same_host_id = host_i == host_j
    )

  hosts <- sort(unique(c(dfw$host_i, dfw$host_j)))

  map_dfr(hosts, function(h) {

    # H–H pairs
    hh <- dfw %>%
      filter(host_i == h, host_j == h)

    # H–other pairs
    h_other <- dfw %>%
      filter((host_i == h & host_j != h) |
             (host_j == h & host_i != h))

    if (nrow(hh) < 5 || nrow(h_other) < 5) {
      return(tibble(
        State = State,
        host = h,
        n_HH = nrow(hh),
        n_Hother = nrow(h_other),
        mean_HH = NA_real_,
        mean_Hother = NA_real_,
        delta = NA_real_
      ))
    }

    tibble(
      State = State,
      host = h,
      n_HH = nrow(hh),
      n_Hother = nrow(h_other),
      mean_HH = mean(hh$sor_core, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_Hother = mean(h_other$sor_core, na.rm = TRUE),
      delta = mean_Hother - mean_HH
    )
  })
})

core_host_specific_contrasts

core_host_specific_contrasts %>%
  filter(is.finite(delta)) %>%
  group_by(host) %>%
  summarise(
    n_states = n_distinct(State),
    mean_delta = mean(delta),
    frac_positive = mean(delta > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


```

Core taxa are not universally host-specific.
Host effects on the core are state-dependent, weak, and often secondary to site-level context.

States with positive host contrast (weak host structuring of core):
F8: +0.015
F3: +0.010
F10: +0.001 (negligible)

These are small effects, but they go in the expected direction:
core communities slightly more similar within host than across hosts (within site).

Interpretation: Some states permit modest host constraint on the core

States with negative host contrast (within-host heterogeneity dominates):
F1: −0.017
F7: −0.029
F6: −0.041
F4: −0.062
F9: −0.002 (≈0)

Within-host core composition is not stabilized; hosts do not enforce a single core configuration, and in some states hosts may even permit more internal variation than across-host comparisons.

This is can happen when hosts span micro-environments, sampling within hosts is heterogeneous, or site-level context dominates over host identity

Host	n_states	mean_delta	frac_positive	Interpretation
ANGE	5	−0.0405	0.20	Consistently within-host heterogeneous
BOER	3	−0.0081	0.67	Weak, inconsistent
BOGR	4	+0.0076	0.50	Essentially noise
BUDA	4	−0.0090	0.50	Noise
SCSC	6	−0.0256	0.17	Consistently heterogeneous

In some states, core composition is modestly constrained by host identity within sites, but in many states within-host heterogeneity equals or exceeds between-host differences. Across states, site-level context exerts a stronger and more consistent influence on core composition than host identity

There is no host that shows positive deltas consistently, across multiple states, with a non-trivial effect size.
Even the “best” case (BOER) is: small magnitude, only 3 states, and inconsistent in sign.
This is exactly what a true null looks like after removing the pooling artifact you identified.

### No host story

Methods: Evaluation of host effects on within-state β-diversity

To assess whether host identity contributes to compositional similarity beyond site-level context, we examined host effects on within-state β-diversity using multiple complementary approaches. All analyses were restricted to sample pairs drawn from the same site to ensure that comparisons were made within a shared environmental context.

Pairwise β-diversity and host contrasts

For each fungal state, Sørensen dissimilarity (β_sor) and its turnover (β_sim) and nestedness (β_sne) components were computed for the full community as well as for prevalence-defined core and satellite taxa. Pairwise comparisons were annotated with host identity and site identity for both members of each pair.

We first quantified host effects using pooled within-site contrasts, comparing mean β-diversity between same-host and different-host sample pairs. This provided a coarse assessment of whether samples from the same host had more similar compositions than samples from different hosts within the same site.

Host-specific contrasts

Because pooled same-host contrasts combine within-host pairs across multiple host types, potentially conflating hosts with different levels of internal heterogeneity, we also evaluated host effects separately for each host type. For each host 𝐻, we compared β-diversity among 𝐻–𝐻 pairs to β-diversity among 𝐻–other host pairs, again restricting comparisons to within-site pairs. This allowed us to determine whether any individual host type exhibited consistently higher within-host similarity than across-host similarity.

Site-level replication

To assess whether host effects were consistent across sites within a state, we calculated host contrasts separately for each site and summarized their direction and magnitude across sites. For each site, the host contrast was defined as the difference between mean β-diversity for different-host pairs and same-host pairs within that site. State-level summaries included the mean and median host contrast across sites, as well as the fraction of sites in which the contrast was positive.

Distributional and variance-based assessments

Because host effects may manifest as changes in dispersion or distributional shape rather than shifts in mean β-diversity, we also compared the variance (SD and IQR) of β-diversity for same-host versus different-host pairs, examined enrichment of same-host pairs among the most similar sample pairs (lowest β tail), and compared full β-diversity distributions using two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests. These analyses were performed separately for core and satellite taxa.

Results: Host effects on β-diversity are weak, inconsistent, and do not define core or satellite organization

Satellite taxa: no evidence for host-stabilized assemblages

Across fungal states, satellite taxa exhibited very high within-site β-diversity dominated by turnover. Mean within-site Sørensen dissimilarity for satellites (β_sor_sat) ranged from 0.79 to 0.85 across states, with turnover components (β_sim_sat) typically accounting for the majority of dissimilarity (e.g., mean β_sim_sat ≈ 0.74–0.82, nestedness components β_sne_sat ≈ 0.02–0.03).

Within this high-turnover regime, same-host and different-host comparisons yielded nearly identical β-diversity values. Pooled within-site host contrasts (defined as mean β_diff-host − mean β_same-host) were uniformly small in magnitude, typically on the order of |Δ| ≤ 0.02 (e.g., F1: Δ = 0.0045, F8: 0.0168, F6: 0.0096), corresponding to relative differences of <3% when scaled by baseline within-site satellite β-diversity (relative Δ ≈ 0.005–0.02).

When host identity was evaluated separately for each host type, no host showed consistently lower satellite β-diversity within host than across hosts. Across five host types, mean host-specific contrasts ranged from approximately −0.03 to +0.02, with no host exhibiting positive contrasts in a majority of states. Variance-based analyses similarly showed no systematic reduction in dispersion for same-host pairs (SD and IQR for same-host and different-host pairs overlapped broadly), and same-host pairs were not consistently enriched among the most similar satellite communities (lowest 10% β tail). Distributional comparisons (Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests) detected occasional differences between same-host and different-host β distributions, but these differences were small and inconsistent in direction.

These results indicate that satellite taxa drive compositional differentiation through near-complete turnover among samples and do not form host-stabilized assemblages, even when comparisons are restricted to within-site pairs and evaluated separately for each host type.

Core taxa: modest β-diversity but no consistent host-specific structure

Core taxa exhibited substantially lower β-diversity than satellites, with mean within-site β_sor_core typically ranging from 0.07 to 0.25 across states. This lower baseline dissimilarity makes host effects more plausible a priori. However, pooled within-site host contrasts for core taxa were small and showed mixed signs across states. Mean pooled contrasts ranged from approximately −0.06 to +0.02 (e.g., F10: +0.0225, F9: +0.0039, F6: −0.0231, F4: −0.0618), corresponding to relative differences of −15% to +16% when scaled by baseline core β-diversity.

When host-specific contrasts were isolated for each host type, no host exhibited consistently lower core β-diversity within host than across hosts across multiple states. Across five host types, mean host-specific contrasts ranged from −0.041 to +0.008, and the fraction of states with positive contrasts never exceeded 0.67 for any host. Two host types (ANGE and SCSC) showed negative contrasts in most states (fraction positive 0.20 and 0.17, respectively), indicating substantial within-host heterogeneity rather than host-stabilized core composition.

Variation among sites does not reveal consistent host organization of the core

Site-level analyses further showed that host contrasts for the core varied markedly in both magnitude and direction among sites within the same state. For example, in state F1 (seven sites), site-specific host contrasts ranged from −0.077 to +0.037, and in state F8 (two sites) from −0.045 to +0.034. Several states exhibited both positive and negative host contrasts across sites, while others showed consistently negative contrasts across all sites examined (e.g., F6 and F7).

Across sites within states, the fraction of sites with positive host contrasts ranged from 0 to 1, with no state exhibiting uniformly positive host effects across sites except those represented by a single site. This variability indicates that host identity does not impose a consistent organizing effect on core composition across sites within a state.

Distributional analyses support the absence of stable host-defined structure

Variance- and distribution-based analyses corroborated these conclusions. For core taxa, same-host pairs did not consistently exhibit reduced dispersion relative to different-host pairs; in several states, within-host variability equaled or exceeded between-host variability. Enrichment of same-host pairs among the most similar core communities was inconsistent and often absent. While distributional differences between same-host and different-host β-diversity were detected in some states (e.g., significant KS tests), these differences did not consistently correspond to greater within-host similarity and varied in direction among states and sites.

Summary interpretation 

Across fungal states, host identity does not define stable compositional assemblages for either satellite or core taxa. Satellite taxa exhibit very high turnover-dominated β-diversity (β_sor ≈ 0.8–0.85) with host contrasts that are negligible relative to baseline dissimilarity (relative Δ typically <2%). Core taxa exhibit lower β-diversity (β_sor ≈ 0.07–0.25), but host effects are weak, inconsistent in sign, and not reproducible across host types or sites. Apparent host effects observed in pooled analyses can be explained by uneven within-host heterogeneity rather than by host-specific stabilization of community composition.

Host effects are evident in richness partitioning and variance structure, but they do not translate into reproducible host-defined β-diversity patterns. Host influence therefore appears to operate through constraints on diversity and variability, rather than through the formation of host-specific composition.



## Dispersion (Part 2.2)

### Scaffolding:

**Two-three outputs here:**

1.  Fig 2C / Fig 2D: dispersion by state (fungi vs bacteria)

2.  SI Table S2.3: betadisper ANOVA + permutation outputs (fungi & bacteria)

3.  Within-site vs between-site contribution

This is a global analysis across states, not inside analyze_one_fungal_state(). It uses whole-kingdom distance matrices, computes distance-to-state spatial median for each sample, and then decomposes variance of those distances into within-site vs between-site components.

```{r}
# Best: get the ANOVA table as a data.frame and compute SS fractions
A <- as.data.frame(stats::anova(disp_fun$betadisper))    # or anova(bd) if bd is in scope
# Make sure the column name for Sum Sq is matched
ss_col <- grep("Sum", names(A), ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)[1]  # typically "Sum Sq"
df_col <- grep("^Df$", names(A), value = TRUE)
f_col  <- grep("F", names(A), value = TRUE)[1]
p_col  <- grep("Pr\\(|p.value|Pr\\(>F\\)", names(A), value = TRUE)[1]

# total SS (sum across all rows in the table)
ss_total <- sum(A[[ss_col]], na.rm = TRUE)

# Add R2-like column
A$prop_ss <- A[[ss_col]] / ss_total

# Nicely formatted reporting object
report_tbl <- A %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "term") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    SumSq = .data[[ss_col]],
    Df    = .data[[df_col]],
    F     = if (!is.null(f_col)) .data[[f_col]] else NA_real_,
    p_val = if (!is.null(p_col)) .data[[p_col]] else NA_real_,
    state_prop_ss = prop_ss
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, Df, SumSq, state_prop_ss, F, p_val)

report_tbl
# Example: get the state term row (if you know its name)
# report_tbl %>% filter(grepl("Fun_sor_clusters|Groups|State", term))


```

ANOVA on distances-to-state-centroids (PERMDISP2) indicates that fungal state identity accounts for 68.5% of the variance in sample–centroid distances (F(9,474) = 114, p = 8.1×10⁻¹¹³; Table 5.1). In other words, fungal states differ in the magnitude of sample–centroid distances (the quantity betadisper measures): some states exhibit systematically larger sample–centroid distances than others. Residual variation (31.5%) represents the remaining sample-to-sample variance not explained by state membership. 

**Interpretation:** fungal states are characterized not only by differences in composition but also by state-specific magnitudes of sample–centroid distance.

## (Part 2.3) Dispersion vs γ_site

Part 2.3 — Regional inventories (γ) 

We have γ columns (Fun_gamma_site, Bac_gamma_site). This section needs:

1.  **Table**: γ_site range by state (and maybe within-state SD)
2.  **Figure**: dispersion vs γ_site, and highlight F1 as counterexample (high γ, low dispersion)

**Approach**: using the dispersion df and joining γ.

```{r}
############################################################
## PART 2.3: gamma vs dispersion
## Requires disp_fun/disp_bac and that sample_data includes gamma columns.
############################################################

summarize_gamma_by_state <- function(disp_df, gamma_site_var, gamma_state_var) {
  if (is.null(disp_df) || !gamma_site_var %in% names(disp_df)) return(NULL)

  disp_df %>%
    filter(is.finite(.data[[gamma_site_var]]), is.finite(dispersion)) %>%
    group_by(State) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      gamma_state = dplyr::first(.data[[gamma_state_var]]),
      mean_gamma_site = mean(.data[[gamma_site_var]]),
      sd_gamma_site   = sd(.data[[gamma_site_var]]),
      min_gamma_site  = min(.data[[gamma_site_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
      max_gamma_site  = max(.data[[gamma_site_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_dispersion = mean(dispersion),
      sd_dispersion   = sd(dispersion),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

# format for display
format_gamma_state_tbl <- function(tbl,
                                   gamma_state_var) {

  tbl %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      # gamma columns: round to whole numbers + thousands separator
      !!gamma_state_var := scales::comma(round(.data[[gamma_state_var]])),
      mean_gamma_site   = scales::comma(round(mean_gamma_site)),
      sd_gamma_site     = scales::comma(round(sd_gamma_site)),
      min_gamma_site    = scales::comma(round(min_gamma_site)),
      max_gamma_site    = scales::comma(round(max_gamma_site)),

      # dispersion: 3 decimal places
      mean_dispersion = scales::number(mean_dispersion, accuracy = 0.001),
      sd_dispersion   = scales::number(sd_dispersion,   accuracy = 0.001)
    )
}

gamma_fun_state_tbl <- if (!is.null(disp_fun)) summarize_gamma_by_state(disp_fun$disp_df, gamma_site_var = gamma_site_fun_var, gamma_state_var = gamma_state_fun_var) else NULL
gamma_bac_state_tbl <- if (!is.null(disp_bac)) summarize_gamma_by_state(disp_bac$disp_df, gamma_site_var = gamma_site_bac_var, gamma_state_var = gamma_state_bac_var) else NULL

gamma_fun_state_tbl_fmt <- format_gamma_state_tbl(
  gamma_fun_state_tbl,
  gamma_state_var = "gamma_state"
)

gamma_bac_state_tbl_fmt <- format_gamma_state_tbl(
  gamma_bac_state_tbl,
  gamma_state_var = "gamma_state"
)

plot_gamma_vs_dispersion <- function(disp_df, gamma_site_var, title = "") {
  ggplot(disp_df, aes(x = .data[[gamma_site_var]], y = dispersion)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
    labs(x = expression(gamma[site]), y = "Dispersion", title = title) +
    theme_bw()
}

fig_gamma_disp_fun <- if (!is.null(disp_fun)) plot_gamma_vs_dispersion(disp_fun$disp_df, gamma_site_fun_var, "Fungi: dispersion vs γ_site") else NULL
fig_gamma_disp_bac <- if (!is.null(disp_bac)) plot_gamma_vs_dispersion(disp_bac$disp_df, gamma_site_bac_var, "Bacteria: dispersion vs γ_site") else NULL
```

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(tibble); library(purrr)
  library(ggplot2)

})


has_fungal_state_results <- !is.null(fungal_state_tbl) &&

# ---- safe formatting ----
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  if (length(x) == 0 || all(!is.finite(x))) return("NA")
  formatC(x[[1]], format = "f", digits = digits)
}

fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 1) {
  if (length(x) == 0 || all(!is.finite(x))) return("NA")
  formatC(x[[1]], format = "f", digits = digits)
}

# ---- safe pulling from the *table* ----
pull_col <- function(df, col, default = NA_real_) {
  if (is.null(df) || !is.data.frame(df) || !col %in% names(df)) return(rep(default, 0))
  df[[col]]
}

pull_one <- function(df, state_id, col, default = NA_real_) {
  if (is.null(df) || !is.data.frame(df)) return(default)
  if (!"State" %in% names(df) || !col %in% names(df)) return(default)
  x <- df[df$State == state_id, col, drop = TRUE]
  if (length(x) == 0) return(default)
  x[[1]]
}

# ---- safe pulling from row *attributes* ----
# (attributes persist because each state result was a 1-row tibble with attrs.)
get_state_row <- function(df, state_id) {
  if (is.null(df) || !is.data.frame(df) || !"State" %in% names(df)) return(NULL)
  hit <- df[df$State == state_id, , drop = FALSE]
  if (nrow(hit) == 0) return(NULL)
  hit
}

# ---------- attribute-aware extraction ----------
get_state_attr <- function(state_row_tbl, attr_name, default = NULL) {
  # state_row_tbl is the 1-row tibble returned by analyze_one_fungal_state()
  a <- attr(state_row_tbl, attr_name, exact = TRUE)
  if (is.null(a)) default else a
}

get_attr <- function(state_row, attr_name, default = NULL) {
  if (is.null(state_row)) return(default)
  x <- attr(state_row, attr_name, exact = TRUE)
  if (is.null(x)) default else x
}


# Optional: a stable “CV” helper for inline text if you want it here too
cv_safe <- function(x) {
  mu <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (!is.finite(mu) || mu == 0) return(NA_real_)
  stats::sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mu
}

# ---------- canonical objects (expect these to exist upstream) ----------
# fungal_state_list: named list of 1-row tibbles, each with attributes
fungal_state_list <- if (exists("fungal_state_list")) fungal_state_list else NULL

has_fungal_state_list <- !is.null(fungal_state_list) && is.list(fungal_state_list) && length(fungal_state_list) > 0

# Build a summary table from the list (attributes will NOT carry through; that is expected)
fungal_state_tbl <- if (has_fungal_state_list) {
  bind_rows(fungal_state_list) %>% as_tibble()
} else {
  NULL
}

has_fungal_state_results <- !is.null(fungal_state_tbl) && is.data.frame(fungal_state_tbl) && nrow(fungal_state_tbl) > 0

fungal_states_present <- if (has_fungal_state_results && "State" %in% names(fungal_state_tbl)) {
  unique(fungal_state_tbl$State)
} else character(0)
```

### Compiler functions columns from `fungal_state_tbl` and attributes from `fungal_state_list`

### Compile tables from attributes and

`build_state_table()` using `fungal_state_tbl` columns; output = 1 table `build_named_state_tables` using X column sets from `fungal_state_tbl`; output = 1 table

```{r compile-table-columns-functions}
# ============================================================
#  COLUMN-BASED TABLE BUILDER (from fungal_state_tbl)
# ============================================================


# ------------------------------------
# build_state_table()
# ------------------------------------
# COLUMN-BASED table builder for `fungal_state_tbl` (single table input).
#
# Use this when:
#   - You want ONE table for ONE analysis (one set of columns).
#   - You want the same output options as the multi-set builder: wide vs long + renaming.
#
# What it does:
#   1) Selects `State` + your requested metric columns from `fungal_state_tbl`.
#   2) Orders rows by `State` using the ordering already present:
#        - If `State` is a factor: respects its existing levels.
#        - If `State` is character: sorts by its existing values (no new levels invented).
#   3) Returns either:
#        - "wide": State + metric columns
#        - "long": State | metric | value
#   4) Optional renaming:
#        - wide_col_labels: rename wide column headers (old_name -> new_name)
#        - metric_labels:   rename long-form metric labels in the `metric` column
#
# What it needs:
#   - fungal_state_tbl: a tibble/data.frame with a `State` column
#   - cols: character vector of metric column names to extract
#
# Notes:
#   - This function makes no assumptions about State naming (not hard-coded to F1..F10).
#   - If you want a specific order, set `State` factor levels upstream; this will respect them.
build_state_table <- function(fungal_state_tbl,
                              cols,
                              state_col = "State",
                              format = c("wide", "long"),
                              strict = TRUE,
                              wide_col_labels = NULL,
                              metric_labels = NULL) {
  format <- match.arg(format)

  if (!state_col %in% names(fungal_state_tbl)) {
    stop("build_state_table(): missing state column: ", state_col)
  }

  missing <- setdiff(cols, names(fungal_state_tbl))
  if (length(missing) > 0 && strict) {
    stop("build_state_table(): missing requested columns: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  }
  cols_present <- intersect(cols, names(fungal_state_tbl))

  # ---- Wide base: State + metrics ----
  wide_tbl <- fungal_state_tbl %>%
    select(all_of(state_col), all_of(cols_present)) %>%
    arrange(.data[[state_col]])

  # Optional: rename wide headers (presentation only)
  # wide_col_labels: named vector old_name -> new_name
  if (!is.null(wide_col_labels)) {
    ren <- wide_col_labels[names(wide_col_labels) %in% names(wide_tbl)]
    wide_tbl <- wide_tbl %>% rename(!!!ren)
  }

  if (format == "wide") return(wide_tbl)

  # ---- Long: State | metric | value ----
  long_tbl <- wide_tbl %>%
    pivot_longer(-all_of(state_col), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

  # Optional: rename long-form metric labels (rewrite `metric`)
  # metric_labels: named vector old_metric -> displayed_label
  if (!is.null(metric_labels)) {
    map_vec <- metric_labels[long_tbl$metric]
    long_tbl$metric <- ifelse(is.na(map_vec), long_tbl$metric, unname(map_vec))
  }

  long_tbl
}
# ------------------------------------



# ------------------------------------
# build_named_state_tables()
# ------------------------------------
# COLUMN-BASED table builder for `fungal_state_tbl` (multi-set wrapper).
#
# Use this when:
#   - You want MANY tables at once (multiple analyses / column sets),
#     and you want them all processed identically (ordering, long/wide, renaming rules).
#
# What it does:
#   - For each named column set in `column_sets` (e.g., abc = abc_cols, decay = decay_cols):
#       1) Calls `build_state_table()` on `fungal_state_tbl` using that set’s columns.
#       2) Returns the result as a named element in a list (tables$abc, tables$decay, ...).
#
# What it needs:
#   - fungal_state_tbl: a tibble/data.frame with a `State` column and analysis columns
#   - column_sets: named list of character vectors (one vector per analysis)
#
# Output:
#   - Named list of tibbles. Names match `names(column_sets)`.
#
# Notes:
#   - This does NOT assume F1..F10 or any naming pattern.
#   - State ordering is handled inside `build_state_table()`:
#       * factor levels are respected; otherwise character sorting is used.
#   - Renaming behavior:
#       * If `wide_col_labels` / `metric_labels` are named vectors, they apply to ALL sets.
#       * If they are named lists of vectors keyed by set name, each set gets its own map.
build_named_state_tables <- function(fungal_state_tbl,
                                     column_sets,
                                     state_col = "State",
                                     format = c("wide", "long"),
                                     strict = TRUE,
                                     wide_col_labels = NULL,
                                     metric_labels = NULL) {
  format <- match.arg(format)

  stopifnot(is.list(column_sets), length(column_sets) > 0, !is.null(names(column_sets)))

  imap(column_sets, function(cols, set_name) {

    # Per-set label maps (if user provided lists keyed by set name)
    wide_labels_i   <- if (is.list(wide_col_labels)) wide_col_labels[[set_name]] else wide_col_labels
    metric_labels_i <- if (is.list(metric_labels))   metric_labels[[set_name]]   else metric_labels

    build_state_table(
      fungal_state_tbl = fungal_state_tbl,
      cols = cols,
      state_col = state_col,
      format = format,
      strict = strict,
      wide_col_labels = wide_labels_i,
      metric_labels = metric_labels_i
    )
  })
}
# ------------------------------------


```

Column-based compiler examples:

```{r compile-table-columns-examples, eval=FALSE}
# ------------------------------------
# 0. Define column set (ABC)
abc_cols <- c(
  "mean_core_contrib_a",
  "mean_sat_contrib_a",
  "mean_core_contrib_bc",

  fungal_state_tbl = fungal_state_tbl,
  cols = abc_cols,

abc_wide

# --- Rename wide headers (presentation only)
wide_labels <- c(
  mean_core_contrib_a  = "core_A",
```

from `fungal_state_list` attributes: 1. Extract attributes across ALL states - extract_state_attrs_long() 2. \# tidy -\> wide reshaper (category-split metrics) - tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide() 3. Backwards-compatible wrapper - audit_tidy_to_wide()

```{r compile-table-attributes-function}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)

# ============================================================
# 1) Extract attributes across ALL states - extract_state_attrs_long()
# ============================================================

# extract_state_attrs_long()
# --------------------------
# What it does:
#   - Iterates over fungal_state_list (named by State: "F1"..."F10")
#   - For each State:
#       * pulls each requested attribute (e.g., "pair_type_audit_satellite")
#       * coerces to tibble
#       * adds State + attr_name columns
#   - Returns one tidy table:
#       State | attr_name | pair_type | component | n_pairs | mean_beta_* ...
#
# What it needs:
#   - fungal_state_list: named list where each element is a state-level tibble
#                        that has your audit attributes attached
#   - attr_names: which attributes to extract
#
# Options:
#   - keep_missing = FALSE: silently skip missing attributes
#   - keep_missing = TRUE : keep a placeholder row for missing attrs (useful for QA)
extract_state_attrs_long <- function(fungal_state_list,
                                     attr_names,
                                     keep_missing = FALSE) {
  stopifnot(is.list(fungal_state_list), length(fungal_state_list) > 0)
  stopifnot(!is.null(names(fungal_state_list)))

  imap_dfr(fungal_state_list, function(state_obj, st) {

    # For each requested attribute, pull it off this state's object
    bind_rows(map(attr_names, function(a) {
      x <- attr(state_obj, a)

      if (is.null(x)) {
        if (keep_missing) return(tibble(State = st, attr_name = a))
        return(NULL)
      }

      as_tibble(x) %>%
        mutate(State = st, attr_name = a, .before = 1)
    }))

  }) %>%
    # Respect State ordering if you already set it as a factor in names or elsewhere.
    # (If State is character, this is alphabetical, which is fine for F1..F10.)
    arrange(State, attr_name, component, pair_type)
}

# ============================================================
# tidy -> wide reshaper (category-split metrics) - tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide()
# ============================================================

# tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide()
# --------------------------
# What it does:
#   - General-purpose "audit_tidy_to_wide" for ANY tidy table shaped like:
#       id columns (things that define a row)
#       one categorical column whose levels you want to split across columns
#       one or more metric/value columns you want repeated per category level
#
#   - Produces wide columns named:
#       <metric><sep><category_level>
#     e.g., mean_beta_sor__same_site_same_host
#
# What it needs:
#   - tbl: a data.frame/tibble
#   - metrics: character vector of columns to widen
#   - id_cols: character vector defining unique rows in wide output
#   - category_col: single column whose values become the suffix in new headers
#
# Naming options (presentation only):
#   - metric_labels: named character vector mapping metric -> header label
#   - category_labels: named character vector mapping category value -> header label
#   - header_fn: optional function(metric_name, category_value) -> header string
#       If provided, it overrides metric_labels/category_labels/sep logic.
#   - sep: separator used when constructing headers (ignored if header_fn is provided)
#
# Notes:
#   - This is exactly your audit reshaper, just parameterized and not audit-specific.
#   - If your table already has metric/value in long form, set metrics to the value columns
#     and it will still work; it will pivot_longer those metrics first.
tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide <- function(tbl,
                                      metrics,
                                      id_cols,
                                      category_col,
                                      sep = "__",
                                      metric_labels = NULL,
                                      category_labels = NULL,
                                      header_fn = NULL) {

  needed <- unique(c(id_cols, category_col, metrics))
  missing <- setdiff(needed, names(tbl))
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop("tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide(): missing columns: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  }

  out <- tbl

  # Optional: relabel category values (e.g., shorten pair_type levels for headers)
  if (!is.null(category_labels)) {
    map_vec <- category_labels[out[[category_col]]]
    out[[category_col]] <- ifelse(is.na(map_vec), out[[category_col]], unname(map_vec))
  }

  # Helper: choose the metric part of the header
  metric_hdr <- function(m) {
    if (is.null(metric_labels)) return(m)
    if (!is.null(metric_labels[[m]])) return(unname(metric_labels[[m]]))
    m
  }

  out %>%
    select(all_of(id_cols), all_of(category_col), all_of(metrics)) %>%
    pivot_longer(all_of(metrics), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(
      metric = vapply(metric, metric_hdr, character(1)),
      colname = if (!is.null(header_fn)) {
        # Full control over header construction
        mapply(header_fn, metric, .data[[category_col]], USE.NAMES = FALSE)
      } else {
        # Default: <metric><sep><category>
        paste(metric, .data[[category_col]], sep = sep)
      }
    ) %>%
    select(all_of(id_cols), colname, value) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = colname, values_from = value) %>%
    arrange(across(all_of(id_cols)))
}

# ============================================================
# Backwards-compatible wrapper - audit_tidy_to_wide()
# ============================================================

# If you like the audit name, keep a thin wrapper so existing calls stay readable.
audit_tidy_to_wide <- function(audit_tbl,
                               metrics,
                               id_cols = c("State", "attr_name", "component"),
                               category_col = "pair_type",
                               sep = "__",
                               metric_labels = NULL,
                               category_labels = NULL,
                               header_fn = NULL) {
  tidy_splitmetrics_to_wide(
    tbl = audit_tbl,
    metrics = metrics,
    id_cols = id_cols,
    category_col = category_col,
    sep = sep,
    metric_labels = metric_labels,
    category_labels = category_labels,
    header_fn = header_fn
  )
}

# Example: pair-type audit
# ============================================================

#   category_col = "pair_type",
#   category_labels = pair_type_labels,
#   metric_labels = metric_labels
# )
```

### Attribute-dependent text (e.g., pulling `alpha_beta_coupling`)

paragraph that depends on the *attribute* `alpha_beta_coupling`, you need to:

1.  access the per-state row (`get_state_row()`), then
2.  `get_attr()`.

Example skeleton:

```{r build-coupling-sentence, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
coupling_sentence <- ""

if (exists("has_fungal_state_results") && isTRUE(has_fungal_state_results) &&
    exists("fungal_states_present") && "F1" %in% fungal_states_present) {

  f1_row <- get_state_row(fungal_state_tbl, "F1")
  coupling <- get_attr(f1_row, "alpha_beta_coupling", default = NULL)

  if (is.null(coupling) || !is.list(coupling) || is.null(coupling$summary_tbl)) {
    coupling_sentence <- "*(α–β coupling will render once alpha_beta_coupling attributes are present.)*"
  } else {
    tbl <- coupling$summary_tbl

    # NOTE: edit these selectors to match your finalized column names
    r2_sor <- tbl$r2[tbl$beta_metric == "sor_full" & tbl$delta == "alpha_total"]
    r2_sim <- tbl$r2[tbl$beta_metric == "sim_full" & tbl$delta == "alpha_total"]

    # safe formatting even if missing
    r2_sor <- ifelse(length(r2_sor) == 0 || is.na(r2_sor[1]), NA, r2_sor[1])
    r2_sim <- ifelse(length(r2_sim) == 0 || is.na(r2_sim[1]), NA, r2_sim[1])

    if (is.na(r2_sor) || is.na(r2_sim)) {
      coupling_sentence <- "*(α–β coupling summary table present, but expected rows were not found.)*"
    } else {
      coupling_sentence <- paste0(
        "Within F1, β_sor increased with |Δα_total| (R² = ", fmt(r2_sor, 2),
        "), while β_sim showed weaker coupling to richness differences (R² = ",
        fmt(r2_sim, 2), ")."
      )
    }
  }
}
```

### Table compiling

#### Compile a single decay summary table from attributes

```{r}
############################################################
## RESULTS TABLE: compile decay summaries from per-state attributes
############################################################
fungal_decay_tbl <- NULL
if (has_fungal_state_results) {
  fungal_decay_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(fungal_state_tbl$State, function(st) {
    row <- get_state_row(fungal_state_tbl, st)
    dec <- get_attr(row, "decay", default = NULL)
    if (is.null(dec) || is.null(dec$decay_summary)) return(NULL)
    dec$decay_summary %>% dplyr::mutate(State = st)
  }))
}

# Now Part 2.8 can do real inline ranges on fungal_decay_tbl$pseudo_r2.
```

#### Compile a single α–β coupling summary table from attributes

```{r}
############################################################
## RESULTS TABLE: compile α–β coupling summaries from per-state attributes
############################################################
fungal_coupling_tbl <- NULL
if (has_fungal_state_results) {
  fungal_coupling_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(fungal_state_tbl$State, function(st) {
    row <- get_state_row(fungal_state_tbl, st)
    cpl <- get_attr(row, "alpha_beta_coupling", default = NULL)
    if (is.null(cpl) || is.null(cpl$summary_tbl)) return(NULL)
    cpl$summary_tbl %>% dplyr::mutate(State = st)
  }))
}
```
